newsitem.title: USA: Dying man misses end of Fla. assisted suicide suit.
newsitem.headline: Dying man misses end of Fla. assisted suicide suit.

text.p: A dying AIDS patient missed closing arguments in his assisted suicide lawsuit against Florida Monday and may not live long enough to benefit from a favourable decision, his doctor said.
Charles Hall, 35, was "simply in too much pain" to remain in court for closing arguments, said Dr. Cecil McIver, the physician who would help Hall end his life should the court approve his request.

Hall, who testified on the opening day of the trial, returned to his home in Beverly, Florida, to await a decision, McIver said. He was being given morphine around the clock to control bone pain associated with his illness.

McIver said he doubted if Hall would live long enough to benefit if the court sides with him. However, "we are allies in a common cause. The outcome of this case may benefit many others," McIver said before closing arguments began in the week-long trial.

Hall and two other terminally ill men sued the state in February 1996, asking that McIver, a Jupiter, Florida, physician, be spared from prosecution for helping them end their lives if their pain became intolerable.
Robert Cron, 72, and Charles Castonguay, 65, both died of cancer last year. The two were dropped as plaintiffs Monday because their cases had become moot.

Hall, who contracted AIDS in 1981 through a blood transfusion, testified last week that he wanted to avoid a lingering death and envisioned an assisted suicide in which McIver would prescribe an overdose of drugs for him.

West Palm Beach attorney Robert Rivas said it could take at least two weeks for Judge S. Joseph Davis to rule. He must decide if a 128-year-old Florida law prohibiting "assisted self murder" violates Hall's rights under the 1981 privacy amendment to the Florida constitution.
In closing arguments, assistant state attorney Michael Gross said any benefit to Hall would be outweighed by the risk to vulnerable people -- the poor, elderly, minorities and disabled.
"They could become unwilling victims of assisted suicide," he said, arguing that the state had a duty to preserve life, prevent suicide and maintain high ethical standards in the medical profession.
"If you should find in favour of (Hall and McIver), it could lead to a license to kill. That would be contrary to a state law which makes euthanasia a crime," he said.
But West Palm Beach attorney Robert Rivas, representing Hall, argued that the case could not have that effect. He said it involved only one terminally ill patient.
"This case is about Hall's right to make a choice about how he will die. Given a chance, between dying and not dying, he would choose not to die," Rivas said.
